nameStory: This charming shrub gets its "old fashioned" name because it was a beloved staple in grandmother's gardens from the Victorian era through the mid-1900s. The genus Weigela honors Christian Ehrenfried Weigel, an 18th-century German scientist and botanist. Though it fell out of favor for a while, this reliable bloomer has made a comeback in modern landscapes.
description: Old Fashioned Weigela is a graceful, arching deciduous shrub that typically grows 6-9 feet tall and wide. In late spring, it puts on a spectacular flower show with masses of funnel-shaped pink blooms that cover the branches. The oval, pointed leaves are a fresh green color and grow opposite each other along the stems. This hardy shrub from eastern Asia has become a naturalized garden escape in some New England areas.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tubular, funnel-shaped flowers about 1 inch long in clusters of 2-3, typically pink to rose-colored with five flared petals that feel papery to touch

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Oval leaves 2-4 inches long with pointed tips, arranged opposite each other on stems, with a slightly rough texture and prominent veining

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Arching, fountain-like form with branches that gracefully bend downward, creating a rounded, spreading shrub

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small, dry capsules that split open to release tiny seeds, not particularly showy or noticeable

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Older stems have light brown bark that peels in thin strips, while young shoots are smooth and green to reddish-brown

habitat: Found as garden escapes in residential areas, along roadsides, and at forest edges throughout New England. Prefers well-drained soils in full sun to partial shade, often persisting around old homesites or spreading from nearby cultivated plantings. Most commonly spotted in southern New England where winters are milder.

seasonality.spring: Peak bloom time in late May to early June when masses of pink tubular flowers cover the arching branches, creating the year's most spectacular display.
seasonality.summer: Fresh green foliage fills out the shrub after flowers fade, and you might spot the small, inconspicuous seed capsules developing.
seasonality.fall: Leaves may turn yellowish before dropping, though fall color is not particularly striking compared to native shrubs.
seasonality.winter: Bare branches reveal the characteristic arching growth pattern, with light brown peeling bark on older stems and visible opposite bud arrangement.

funFact: Weigela flowers are actually designed to change color as they age - they start out pale pink or white, then deepen to rose or red to signal to pollinators that the nectar supply is running low, like a natural traffic light system!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with native azaleas or other flowering shrubs, but Weigela's tubular flowers and opposite leaves distinguish it from azaleas, which have funnel-shaped flowers and alternate leaves. Remember: Weigela has opposite leaves like the honeysuckle family it belongs to.
contextualKnowledge: Though called "old fashioned," this plant is actually a relatively recent introduction to North America, arriving in the 1800s from Asia. It's sometimes considered invasive in certain areas, so check local guidelines before planting.
compareHints: Since this is the only Weigela commonly found in New England, compare it to other members of the honeysuckle family like native honeysuckle vines or elderberry shrubs. Unlike climbing honeysuckles, Weigela is strictly a shrub, and unlike elderberry, it has simple (not compound) leaves and tubular rather than flat-topped flower clusters.
